messages.content: I want to determine when black-box language-model evaluations can distinguish paraphrased benchmark contamination from genuine generalization, even when the training distributions are unknown. The evaluation should achieve at least 80% detection power at 5% false positives against uncontaminated, capability-matched models. I also want the identifiability assumptions stated explicitly, including which contamination regimes would be observationally indistinguishable from genuine generalization.

That separates two questions: whether contamination and genuine generalization can produce different observable behavior at all, and whether an evaluation can detect that difference reliably enough to meet the stated threshold. The target is at least 80% detection power while keeping false positives at 5% against uncontaminated, capability-matched models. It is a target for the evaluation, not a result that follows merely from defining contamination.

The unknown training distributions are central. Black-box responses reveal behavior, not the provenance of the training material. A model's success on benchmark questions—even on paraphrases—does not by itself say whether it encountered related benchmark content or generalized from other learning.
What does capability matching contribute to that comparison?

It makes the false-positive comparison more demanding and more relevant. The uncontaminated models are meant to have comparable capability, so a detector cannot simply label strong benchmark performance as contamination while treating lower-performing models as the clean baseline.

Capability matching does not, by itself, solve attribution. Two comparably capable models might differ in their black-box behavior for reasons other than benchmark exposure. The identifiability assumptions must say what variation is allowed among uncontaminated, capability-matched models and what observable difference is being attributed to paraphrased benchmark contamination.
So the 5% figure is not just a general error rate?

Right. It constrains false accusations specifically for the relevant clean comparison: uncontaminated, capability-matched models. Detection power is the probability of flagging contamination when the specified contaminated case is present; the requirement is at least 80%. A meaningful claim needs to say which contaminated cases that power covers and how those probabilities are evaluated.

If the 80% target is intended to apply to every possible form of paraphrased contamination under entirely unrestricted, unknown training distributions, there is an immediate identifiability problem: some contaminated and uncontaminated models can be behaviorally identical from the evaluator's perspective.
Can you state that identifiability problem without assuming access to the training data?

Consider everything the black-box evaluation could observe: the model's responses to its permitted queries, including any randomness in those responses. If a contaminated model and an uncontaminated, capability-matched model induce the same distribution over all those observations, no rule using those observations can distinguish them. Any event called a positive detection has the same probability for both models.

Consequently, a rule limited to 5% false positives for that clean model can have at most 5% detection power for the observationally identical contaminated model. This is a limit on inference from black-box behavior, not a claim that either model has a particular training history.
Does exact equality of observable behavior have to hold for the problem to be difficult?

No. Exact equality is the clearest impossibility case, but near-equality also matters for the 80% target. If the observable distributions are so close that no detection event can be much more likely under the contaminated model than under a capability-matched clean model, keeping false positives at 5% leaves little room to reach 80% power.

In the usual total-variation formulation, 80% power at 5% false positives requires a difference of at least 75 percentage points between the probabilities of the chosen detection event. Thus the two observable distributions must be separated by at least 0.75 in total variation for that pair. This is a necessary condition for that pair, not a promise that one evaluation rule will work across every model in a broader class.
I want to be careful about the word “paraphrased.” Why doesn't performance on reworded questions settle the issue?

Because both possibilities can support performance on reworded questions. Exposure to paraphrases of benchmark content might carry over to other phrasings; genuine generalization might do so as well. The absence of an exact string match does not establish that benchmark-related content was absent from training, and the presence of correct answers to reworded questions does not establish that it was present.

The question is whether paraphrased contamination produces an observable pattern that a genuinely generalizing, capability-matched model could not plausibly reproduce under the stated assumptions. Without such a distinction, rewording changes the observations available but does not identify their cause.
What assumptions would have to be explicit before making a positive detection claim?

At minimum, the claim needs a defined set of permitted black-box observations and two clearly scoped classes: uncontaminated, capability-matched models and models with the form of paraphrased benchmark contamination being investigated. It also needs a bound on how much the relevant observations can vary within the clean class. Otherwise an apparent contamination signal might simply be ordinary variation among clean models of comparable capability.

Most importantly, there must be an assumption connecting the specified contamination to a distinguishable behavioral effect—one that cannot be reproduced by the allowed clean models—and enough separation for the proposed error targets. These are identifiability assumptions, not findings that contamination necessarily leaves such an effect.
Isn't a distinguishable effect almost the same as assuming the answer?

It would be, if asserted without qualification or presented as evidence. Stating the assumption serves a different purpose: it makes clear what a black-box conclusion is conditional on. Unknown training distributions do not supply a universal behavioral signature of paraphrased exposure. One must either restrict the competing possibilities enough for an observable distinction to exist or acknowledge that the histories cannot be separated from behavior alone.

A useful formulation distinguishes an assumption that a difference exists from a demonstrated ability to detect it. Even if contaminated and clean models are observably different in principle, their differences may be too small, too inconsistent, or differently directed across models for a single evaluation to attain 80% power at the specified 5% false-positive rate.
What does “too inconsistently directed” mean in this setting?

The contaminated class could contain models whose observable deviations from clean models differ from one another. One might show a behavior that another does not, while an uncontaminated, capability-matched model might show something similar to either. Distinguishing each contaminated model from some clean model separately does not automatically produce one detection rule that distinguishes the whole class while controlling false positives across the clean class.

That is why the scope of the power statement matters. Power for a particular specified contamination regime is not the same claim as power for all regimes that might be called paraphrased benchmark contamination.
Then how should the observationally indistinguishable regimes be characterized?

They are regimes in which contamination makes no difference to the distribution of permitted black-box observations relative to at least one uncontaminated, capability-matched alternative. For example, benchmark-related paraphrases could have been present in training without changing the model's responses in a detectable way. Alternatively, their effect on responses could coincide with behavior that an allowed clean model achieves through generalization. Those are conceptual possibilities, not assertions about any particular model.

A broader near-indistinguishable regime comprises cases whose observable effects are so small, or so entangled with permissible clean-model variation, that the required 80% power and 5% false-positive rate cannot both be met. Such cases need not be exactly behaviorally identical to defeat the specified performance target.
Would asking more black-box questions necessarily move a case out of that regime?

Not necessarily. More observations can help when a real, accessible behavioral difference exists and additional queries reveal it. They cannot recover a training history that has no distinct observable implication within the allowed black-box interaction. If the contaminated and clean alternatives give the same distributions for every permitted query and response sequence, additional interaction remains uninformative about which history occurred.

For nearly indistinguishable cases, the answer depends on how much separation additional observations can create. The fact that more queries are available is not, on its own, an identifiability assumption or an 80%-power guarantee.
How does the unknown training distribution affect what counts as a clean alternative?

It means the evaluator cannot silently assume that an uncontaminated model lacks other training material that would support the same answers or response patterns. “Uncontaminated” specifies the absence of the benchmark-related exposure at issue; it does not mean incapable of answering the benchmark. Capability matching makes that especially important.

If the allowed clean training distributions are broad enough to yield every behavior that the contaminated class yields, then black-box observations alone cannot establish provenance. Any positive claim must therefore say which alternatives are excluded or constrained, and why the resulting clean comparison remains the one relevant to the 5% false-positive requirement.
Is it fair to say the aim is conditional rather than a universal test for contamination?

Yes. The aim is to determine *when* a black-box evaluation can make the distinction, not to presume that it always can. For a specified, identifiable contamination regime, the performance objective is at least 80% detection power at 5% false positives against uncontaminated, capability-matched models. For regimes observationally equivalent to genuine generalization, that objective cannot be achieved using only the permitted black-box evidence.

The boundary between those statements should be explicit: what observations are available, what models and training distributions are admitted as alternatives, what behavioral separation is assumed or established, and whether the claimed power covers all contaminated models in scope or a narrower subset.
I don't want a high benchmark score to be treated as evidence of provenance just because the items are paraphrased.

That caution is consistent with the goal. A high score is an observation about performance. Paraphrased benchmark contamination and genuine generalization are possible explanations, and unknown training distributions leave open other ways an uncontaminated, similarly capable model could attain that performance. The inference requires more than relabeling good performance as exposure.

The proposed distinction has to survive comparison with clean models matched on capability, under the stated 5% false-positive constraint. If it cannot, the appropriate black-box conclusion is limited: the behavior may be compatible with contamination, but it does not distinguish contamination from genuine generalization.
And if contamination has an observable effect, can I immediately claim the 80% target is feasible?

No. An observable effect establishes a possible basis for distinction, but the numerical target is stronger. The effect must permit a detection rule that reaches at least 80% power for the contaminated cases in scope while producing no more than 5% false positives for the relevant uncontaminated, capability-matched models. The rule must work against the specified uncertainty in both classes, rather than only against one convenient pair.

Conversely, if a contaminated model is observationally identical to an admitted clean comparator, the 80% target is impossible for that model under the 5% constraint. Those statements delineate what the evaluation would need to establish without claiming that it has already done so.
So the identifiability assumptions should identify the observable gap, not merely assert that contamination happened?

Exactly. Contamination is about training history; detection from black-box evaluation is about observable consequences of that history relative to genuine generalization. An explicit account would say which paraphrased benchmark exposures are in scope, which uncontaminated models of comparable capability are valid comparators, and what response-level distinction remains after allowing for their variation.

It should also state the limit: when contaminated and clean alternatives produce the same permitted observations—or observations insufficiently separated for the stated error rates—their different histories are observationally indistinguishable for this purpose. That limit is part of determining when the distinction can be made, not a failure to define the question.

I’d like to pursue a comparison between paraphrase-stable benchmark error fingerprints and private isomorphic twins. The comparison would be calibrated against capability-matched clean models, with identifiability bounds derived alongside it. How should I understand that proposal?

The proposal looks for a *pattern of mistakes*, rather than treating a high benchmark score as evidence of exposure. A paraphrase-stable error fingerprint would be a recognizable pattern associated with benchmark items that persists when those items are reworded. Private isomorphic twins provide corresponding cases with the same relevant task structure, so the comparison asks whether the pattern is specific to the benchmark side or is also what comparable performance on equivalent tasks would produce.

Capability-matched clean models provide the reference for deciding how unusual that contrast is without contamination. The identifiability bounds would then state what the comparison can and cannot establish from black-box observations under its assumptions. This is a proposed way to investigate the distinction, not a finding that such fingerprints exist or are diagnostic.
Why focus on errors instead of just comparing how often the model gets benchmark items and twins right?

Overall accuracy can reflect capability on the underlying task. A model that generalizes well could do well on both benchmark items and structurally equivalent twins. Error fingerprints ask a narrower question: whether *which mistakes occur* and how they persist across paraphrases carry information that aggregate scores miss.

That does not make mistakes inherently evidence of contamination. A genuinely generalizing model may also have stable weaknesses. The proposed comparison is useful only if a benchmark-linked error pattern differs from the patterns expected for private isomorphic twins and from the variation seen among uncontaminated, capability-matched models.
What work are the private isomorphic twins doing?

They provide a counterpoint to the benchmark items without simply asking the same benchmark questions again. “Isomorphic” calls for preservation of the task-relevant structure; “private” indicates that the twin items are not being treated as publicly exposed benchmark material. Conceptually, they help ask whether a model’s behavior transfers to equivalent cases or is unusually tied to the benchmark cases.

Neither property is automatic. A twin that differs in task difficulty would weaken the comparison, and calling an item private does not by itself prove anything about every model’s training distribution. Those are conditions the proposal would need to address rather than conclusions supplied by the name.
Is the fingerprint meant to be stable across paraphrases of an individual item, or across the benchmark more generally?

The proposal’s wording leaves the precise scope to be defined. At minimum, “paraphrase-stable” means that the relevant error pattern is not just an artifact of one surface wording. A fingerprint could be described at the level of corresponding responses or across a collection of items, but whichever level is chosen needs to be specified before interpreting a match.

The key comparison remains the same: does the observed stability on benchmark paraphrases tell us something that equally structured private twins and capability-matched clean models do not already explain? Calling a pattern a fingerprint should not quietly assume that it is unique to contamination.
If benchmark and twin behavior differ, wouldn't that be enough?

It would be an observation to explain, not enough on its own to attribute training history. Even isomorphic cases may elicit different behavior for reasons the black-box evaluation does not isolate. The comparison needs calibration against clean models of comparable capability: how much benchmark–twin disparity can occur without the contamination at issue?

Only a difference that can be distinguished from that clean variation could support a detection claim. The identifiability assumptions would need to state why the remaining difference is attributable to the specified paraphrased benchmark contamination rather than to an allowed form of genuine generalization.
How should the calibration relate to the requirement of 5% false positives?

The clean, capability-matched models define the relevant false-positive comparison. If a rule flags a benchmark-linked fingerprint, its positive rate among those uncontaminated models must be at most 5% for the stated target. Calibration means judging the candidate signal against that reference, rather than treating any visually striking pattern as suspicious.

The other half of the goal remains at least 80% detection power for the contamination regime being claimed. Calibration against clean models addresses false accusations; it does not, by itself, show that contaminated models will exhibit a detectable fingerprint often enough to reach that power.
Would capability matching erase the signal by making the models too similar?

Not necessarily, but it makes the signal answer the right question. If a proposed fingerprint reflects only a broad capability difference, matching capability would expose that limitation. If there is a contamination-linked contrast that persists among comparably capable models, matching need not erase it.

The proposal does not establish which outcome occurs. It uses capability-matched clean models so that a putative contamination effect cannot be inferred merely from general differences in competence.
I’m concerned that stable errors may be evidence of ordinary generalization rather than memorized benchmark material.

That concern belongs at the center of the comparison. Stable errors can arise from stable approaches to a task, whether or not benchmark material was present in training. A model might reproduce the same kind of mistake on both benchmark paraphrases and their isomorphic twins because the underlying difficulty is shared.

The proposed signal therefore cannot be “stable errors imply contamination.” It would have to be a specific contrast between benchmark-linked stability and twin behavior that clean, capability-matched models rarely exhibit, under stated assumptions about what the twins preserve. Even then, the inference is conditional on the set of genuine-generalization alternatives admitted.
Does it matter whether the twins are genuinely comparable, rather than just similar-looking questions?

Yes. The comparison relies on their being isomorphic in the aspects relevant to the inference. If the twins change what capability is required, a benchmark–twin gap could reflect that change rather than benchmark exposure. If they are equivalent only superficially, agreement or disagreement may be hard to interpret.

The proposal therefore needs a defensible meaning of isomorphism and an account of how much behavioral variation equivalent cases may produce for clean models. It does not require assuming that all such cases yield identical responses; the calibration is meant to make room for ordinary variation.
And why does privacy matter if training distributions are unknown anyway?

Privacy gives the twins their intended role as comparators not drawn from the benchmark material whose possible exposure is under investigation. But unknown training distributions limit what privacy alone can establish. An evaluator cannot infer from a label that no model encountered related content or learned a way to solve the twins.

So privacy supports the design of the contrast, while identifiability still depends on explicit assumptions about exposure, equivalence, and what uncontaminated models could do. It should not be used as a shortcut to declaring benchmark–twin differences contamination-specific.
What would an identifiability bound describe here?

It would describe a limit on distinguishing contaminated from uncontaminated, capability-matched behavior using the observations generated by this comparison. The observations include whatever benchmark-paraphrase and private-twin error patterns the proposed evaluation permits. If contaminated and clean alternatives induce the same distribution over those patterns, no black-box rule based on them can distinguish the alternatives.

If their distributions are merely close, a bound can express how large a detection advantage is possible while respecting the clean-model false-positive limit. Deriving that bound keeps a promising-looking fingerprint separate from a justified claim about provenance.
Can you connect that directly to the 80% power and 5% false-positive objective?

For a given detection event, reaching 80% power while holding false positives to 5% requires that event to be at least 75 percentage points more likely under the contaminated case than under the clean comparator. In terms of the distributions over the permitted black-box observations, that entails at least that much separation in total variation for the pair. It is a necessary condition, not sufficient evidence that the proposed fingerprint comparison supplies such an event.

The distinction is also important across classes of models: favorable separation for one contaminated–clean pair does not automatically give a single calibrated rule with at least 80% power for every contamination regime in scope.
Suppose the fingerprint comparison looks the same for a contaminated model and a clean model. What can the evaluation say?

For that pair, it cannot determine which training history produced the behavior from the proposed observations. If their full permitted black-box observations are the same, the limitation holds for any black-box evaluation with those observations, not just for this particular fingerprint comparison. If only the fingerprint comparison is the same, another permitted observation might in principle distinguish them, but the proposed signal does not.

That distinction helps keep the identifiability claim appropriately scoped. A failure of this comparison to distinguish histories need not be a claim that no conceivable observation could ever do so.
Could contamination leave no distinctive error fingerprint at all?

Yes, as a possibility the identifiability analysis must allow. Benchmark-related paraphrases could have been present in training while the model’s resulting error behavior matches what a genuinely generalizing, capability-matched model could produce. Contamination could also have an observable effect that does not take the form of a paraphrase-stable benchmark error fingerprint.

The proposal investigates a particular possible signal. It should characterize regimes in which that signal is absent or indistinguishable, rather than assuming that all paraphrased benchmark contamination leaves the same trace.
I also don’t want the twin comparison to turn into a rule that says any benchmark advantage proves contamination.

It should not. A benchmark advantage, like an error pattern, is behavior requiring interpretation. The proposed comparison is strongest as a conditional question: is there a paraphrase-stable, benchmark-specific error fingerprint that differs from what private isomorphic twins and capability-matched clean models would lead us to expect?

A positive-looking contrast would still need the stated calibration and identifiability assumptions before it could support a claim at the 80% power and 5% false-positive targets. Without those conditions, the comparison may describe a behavioral difference without identifying its source.
Does calibrating on clean models establish that the twins are isomorphic?

No. Those address different parts of the argument. Isomorphism concerns whether the benchmark items and private twins preserve the relevant task structure. Clean-model calibration concerns the distribution of comparison outcomes that can occur without the specified contamination, among models of comparable capability.

Calibration might reveal that clean models often differ between the two sets, which would affect how informative a contrast is. But it cannot, by itself, establish that the twins are structurally equivalent or that a remaining contrast must be caused by training exposure.
What if the clean models themselves show persistent error patterns on benchmark paraphrases?

Then persistence alone is not a discriminating signal. The calibration must account for the paraphrase-stable patterns clean models can exhibit, including how those patterns compare with behavior on the twins. The question is not whether an error fingerprint is memorable to an observer, but whether it is sufficiently distinct from the clean, capability-matched reference to support the specified false-positive and power claims.

That is also why defining the fingerprint matters: an imprecise description can make ordinary clean-model behavior look special after the fact.
So the bound should account for the clean class, not just a single favored clean model?

If the claim is against uncontaminated, capability-matched models as a class, yes. A comparison that distinguishes contamination from one particular clean model might not distinguish it from another allowed clean model with similar benchmark and twin behavior. The false-positive requirement and the identifiability bound should have scopes consistent with the models the conclusion purports to cover.

Likewise, the 80% power claim needs a clear scope on the contaminated side. The proposed comparison might be informative for some regimes and observationally uninformative for others; a bound can make that difference explicit without treating either possibility as an observed result.
Can you put the whole proposal in one careful statement, without making it sound as though the evaluation has already succeeded?

The proposal is to compare error fingerprints that persist across paraphrases of benchmark items with behavior on private, task-isomorphic twins, then interpret any resulting contrast using uncontaminated, capability-matched models as the calibration reference. Alongside that comparison, derive identifiability bounds specifying the assumptions and observable separation needed to distinguish paraphrased benchmark contamination from genuine generalization—and specifying regimes in which the two remain observationally indistinguishable.

Whether this approach can attain at least 80% detection power at 5% false positives is the question to assess, not a conclusion built into the proposal.
When does excess agreement on rare benchmark errors across paraphrases, relative to private twins, identify contamination rather than shared reasoning?

Only when that excess is difficult to explain by the allowed forms of shared reasoning and ordinary clean-model variation. Agreement means that the same error persists across rewordings; rarity means the error is uncommon under some specified reference; and “excess” means it occurs more on benchmark paraphrases than on corresponding private twins. None of those properties, separately or together, establishes training history without assumptions about what uncontaminated, capability-matched models could do.

The central question is whether the observed contrast is distinctive of the contamination at issue, rather than a stable way of reasoning about those particular cases.
Why wouldn't an unusual, repeated wrong answer be distinctive enough?

An unusual wrong answer can still have an ordinary explanation. If several phrasings preserve the feature that leads a model astray, repeating the error may demonstrate consistency of its reasoning, not exposure to the benchmark. And an error that is rare among the cases examined may be less rare among genuinely comparable clean models.

The comparison with private twins matters because it asks whether the same reasoning difficulty carries over to equivalent cases. But even a benchmark–twin difference needs interpretation: it might reflect a contamination effect, or it might reflect a difference between the cases that the notion of isomorphism has not captured.
So what, exactly, has to be rare?

It should be clear whether “rare” refers to the erroneous answer itself, the pattern of repeating that error across paraphrases, or the *contrast* between that repetition on benchmark items and behavior on private twins. Those are different claims. An answer can be rare in isolation while its recurrence on related phrasings is unsurprising once the model's first mistake is known.

For identifying contamination, the relevant rarity is conditional on an appropriate clean comparison: how unusual would the full observed pattern be for an uncontaminated, capability-matched model facing the benchmark paraphrases and corresponding twins? A label of “rare benchmark error” alone does not answer that.
Does agreement across several paraphrases give several independent pieces of evidence?

Not automatically. The paraphrases are connected by the same underlying item. If they preserve the cause of a particular mistake, agreement may be highly dependent: once the model errs on one version, its behavior on the others may be predictable without invoking contamination.

Repeated agreement can still be informative, but its evidential weight depends on how often that *joint pattern* occurs under genuine generalization. Treating every paraphrase as an independent surprise would overstate what the black-box observations distinguish.
What would make the twins a meaningful comparison for this question?

They would need to preserve the task-relevant structure that could support the same reasoning and the same kind of mistake. Otherwise, lower agreement on the twins may simply mean they do not present the same difficulty. The comparison is informative when a shared-reasoning explanation would predict similar error behavior on the twins, while the specified contamination explanation would predict a benchmark-specific departure.

Those predictions have to be justified as assumptions or examined through clean-model calibration. Calling the twins isomorphic expresses their intended role; it does not eliminate every possible behavioral difference between them and the benchmark cases.
What if the benchmark error repeats across paraphrases, but the corresponding twin errors don't repeat?

That is the kind of excess agreement the question asks about. It could favor contamination *if* benchmark exposure is expected to produce that asymmetry and the allowed shared-reasoning accounts do not. But the observed asymmetry alone does not establish those premises.

For instance, a model might respond consistently to a particular feature retained by the benchmark paraphrases that is not equally salient in the twins. That would be a behavioral explanation without requiring contamination. The task is to determine whether such clean explanations remain plausible within the comparison being made.
Does “private” rule out that alternative?

No. Privacy concerns the twins' role as comparison material; it does not make their wording, difficulty, or the model's interpretation identical to the benchmark items. Nor does it reveal the model's unknown training distribution. A private twin can help distinguish benchmark-specific behavior from transfer to equivalent cases, but its privacy is not, on its own, proof that a difference was caused by benchmark contamination.
Then where do capability-matched clean models enter the answer?

They help define what shared reasoning and other uncontaminated behavior can look like at a comparable level of ability. If such models also show repeated rare-looking benchmark errors relative to the twins, that pattern is not specific to contamination. If the pattern is genuinely uncommon among the relevant clean models, it becomes a more promising signal—but it still depends on whether those models adequately represent the clean alternatives being allowed.

The point of capability matching is that an apparent fingerprint should not merely distinguish models with different general competence. The comparison is about provenance conditional on comparable capability, not simply about who performs better.
Could clean models share the *same* rare wrong answer for a reason other than contamination?

Yes. They might share an interpretation of the question or a reasoning tendency that leads to that answer. The fact that the answer is wrong and unusual does not make its cause unique. This is especially relevant when the paraphrases preserve the aspect of the item that triggers the interpretation.

To use agreement as an identifying signal, the clean comparison must address the probability of that particular agreement pattern, not just the overall frequency of incorrect answers.
If the clean comparison rarely shows it, have we identified contamination?

Not necessarily. Rarity under a specified clean comparison can support a discriminating rule for that comparison, but attribution still depends on the scope of the clean alternatives. With unknown training distributions, a genuinely generalizing, capability-matched model might produce the same observable pattern even if the particular clean models used for comparison do not.

A careful claim would say which alternatives are covered, what benchmark–twin pattern is being compared, and how strongly that pattern separates the contaminated and clean cases. It should not turn “rare in the chosen reference” into “impossible without contamination.”
What is the distinction between evidence that favors contamination and identification of contamination?

Evidence can shift the comparison toward contamination under stated assumptions without uniquely determining the training history. Identification is a stronger claim: the permitted black-box observations separate contamination from the genuine-generalization alternatives admitted by the analysis.

If an uncontaminated, capability-matched model can have the same distribution of benchmark-paraphrase and twin behaviors as a contaminated one, the pattern cannot identify which history occurred. It may be suggestive relative to a narrower reference while remaining non-identifying under a broader set of possible clean models.
Does the comparison need a prediction about the *direction* of the difference?

Yes, for a specific interpretive claim. “Excess agreement on benchmark errors relative to twins” names a direction, but its causal interpretation still needs a reason that paraphrased benchmark contamination would produce that direction and that shared reasoning would not ordinarily do so under the relevant conditions.

It is not enough to say that the two sets differ and then treat whichever difference appears as contamination. The proposed interpretation concerns a particular contrast; other contrasts might have different explanations.
Could genuine generalization itself be benchmark-specific?

In black-box behavior, it could look that way. A model might find the benchmark cases easier or harder than their twins because of features it has learned to use generally, even if both sets are intended to be isomorphic. That possibility is why the inference cannot rest entirely on the evaluator's intuition that equivalent cases should elicit equivalent behavior.

The relevant assumption must constrain how much benchmark-specific behavior genuine generalization can produce among capability-matched clean models. If it leaves room for the full observed excess agreement, contamination is not identified by that excess.
What about the fact that the errors are rare? Doesn't that constrain the shared-reasoning story?

It can, but only after the reference and conditioning are made clear. A shared-reasoning explanation for a specific rare error might be less plausible than one for a common error. Still, a single underlying misinterpretation can generate the same rare response on many paraphrases. Its recurrence is then a consequence of that shared cause, not repeated independent evidence against generalization.

The informative question is how often the complete, benchmark-specific pattern arises under the allowed clean models, including dependence among the paraphrases and behavior on the twins. Rarity of each component separately need not imply rarity of the pattern in the way an independence assumption would suggest.
Suppose the twins are truly equivalent in the relevant sense. Wouldn't a benchmark-only pattern then prove exposure?

It would remove an important alternative explanation, but “truly equivalent in the relevant sense” has to carry substantial weight. It would need to mean that, under the genuine-generalization alternatives in scope, the observed benchmark-only error agreement is not an ordinary consequence of how the models handle the two sets. If that condition and a contamination-linked behavioral effect are warranted, the pattern can be identifying within that scope.

Structural equivalence alone does not logically force a black-box model to give identical answers to distinct inputs. The inference also needs an account of permissible response variation and of why the particular excess is associated with the specified training exposure.
Is it possible for contamination to be present without producing excess agreement?

Yes. The question concerns when a particular signal identifies contamination, not whether all contamination must produce it. Exposure to paraphrased benchmark material might leave no detectable effect on these errors, or the resulting behavior might look the same as genuine generalization. Conversely, shared reasoning could produce excess agreement without that exposure.

So absence of the signal would not, by itself, establish an uncontaminated training history, just as presence of the signal would not automatically establish contamination.
How should I think about identifiability if those two causes produce exactly the same pattern?

If they produce the same distribution over all observations used in the comparison, the pattern is observationally indistinguishable between them. A decision based solely on those observations must behave the same way for both histories. No amount of confidence in the label “rare error” changes that limit.

If they produce different distributions, distinction may be possible in principle; whether the difference is large and consistent enough to support a useful evaluation is a further question. “Not identical” is weaker than “reliably identifiable.”
Is there a risk of defining the fingerprint after noticing the benchmark errors?

Yes, as a matter of interpretation. If an error pattern is called rare only after selecting it from many observed possibilities, its apparent distinctiveness may not reflect how uncommon the selection process would be for clean models. The relevant clean comparison must encompass what is actually being treated as a positive signal, including the way the pattern is chosen.

That point does not require a particular implementation. It follows from the question itself: identifying contamination requires assessing the excess agreement being used as evidence, rather than only assessing a description of it that became compelling after it was seen.
Can I frame shared reasoning as a competing explanation rather than something to rule out categorically?

That is the careful framing. Shared reasoning is a class of potential explanations for correlated mistakes across paraphrases. The issue is whether the benchmark-versus-twin contrast excludes those explanations sufficiently under explicit assumptions and the relevant clean-model comparison.

You need not claim that uncontaminated models never make rare, repeated errors. Instead, ask whether their permitted behavior can account for the *amount and form* of excess agreement observed. If it can, the pattern does not identify training provenance; if it cannot under justified assumptions, the pattern may support an identification claim within that defined scope.
What should a precise answer to the original question avoid saying?

It should avoid saying that repeated rare benchmark errors are inherently memorization, that private twins are guaranteed to eliminate reasoning differences, or that clean-model rarity proves the absence of every possible genuine-generalization explanation. It should also avoid treating correlated paraphrases as independent confirmations.

The conditional answer is: excess agreement identifies contamination only to the extent that the benchmark and twin comparison preserves the relevant reasoning demands, the clean comparison captures the allowed shared-reasoning behavior of capability-matched models, and the specified contamination produces an observable contrast those clean alternatives cannot reproduce. Where those conditions do not separate the observable behaviors, the excess may be interesting without identifying its cause.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: at 300 items and 30% paraphrase contamination, exchangeable twins and matched controls enable at least 80% rare-error detection power at a 5% false-positive rate. Does that address when excess agreement on rare benchmark errors indicates contamination rather than shared reasoning?

It gives that question a concrete, testable setting, but it remains a hypothesis. The 300 items and 30% paraphrase contamination specify the setting; the proposed use of exchangeable twins and matched controls supplies the comparison. The claim to examine is whether that comparison can detect the specified contamination through rare-error behavior with at least 80% power while holding false positives to 5% among the matched clean controls.

The numbers alone do not establish that result. It depends on whether contamination produces an observable error contrast that shared reasoning among the clean controls does not also produce.
What does “exchangeable twins” need to mean for this hypothesis?

It needs to mean more than that the private twins look similar to the benchmark items. For the relevant uncontaminated comparison, treating a benchmark item and its twin as counterparts should not systematically change the rare-error behavior being used as a signal. Otherwise a benchmark–twin difference could arise without contamination.

Exchangeability is therefore an assumption about the comparison, not an observed consequence of calling the items twins. It must be stated at the level relevant to the proposed error pattern, including agreement across paraphrases, rather than only at the level of overall difficulty.
Are you saying the model has to answer each benchmark item and twin identically?

No. Exchangeability need not mean identical answers on every paired case. It concerns what differences are expected across the comparison under the clean explanation. Individual responses can vary while the benchmark and twin sides remain exchangeable for the error behavior being assessed.

If the hypothesis instead required exact answer-by-answer equality for clean models, that would be a much stronger assumption. The important point is to specify enough equivalence that a systematic *excess* of rare-error agreement on benchmark paraphrases has an interpretable reference.
And what are the matched controls contributing beyond the twins?

The twins supply a within-task contrast. The matched controls show what that contrast can look like for uncontaminated models of comparable capability. Even with well-chosen twins, clean models might sometimes repeat an unusual benchmark error more consistently than a twin error. The controls are the reference for how often a proposed detection rule would flag such behavior without the contamination at issue.

That is how the 5% false-positive condition enters the hypothesis. Exchangeability supports interpretation of the benchmark–twin comparison; matched clean controls support calibration of a rule based on that comparison. Neither alone establishes at least 80% detection power.
Does the 30% contamination figure mean 30% of the answers should show a rare error?

No. The hypothesis says 30% paraphrase contamination, not a 30% rare-error rate or a prediction that each contaminated item will produce a particular response. If the percentage is meant to be an item-level fraction of the 300 items, it corresponds arithmetically to 90 items; that does not tell us how many will yield a detectable fingerprint.

The unit of contamination should be explicit when assessing the hypothesis. In any interpretation, a proportion of contaminated material cannot by itself determine detection power without an assumption about its effect on observable errors.
Why doesn't having 300 items settle the power question?

Because the amount of information is not determined by the item count alone. Errors on paraphrases of an item may be closely related, and the benchmark–twin contrasts may vary in how informative they are. More items can offer more opportunities to observe a difference, but they cannot create one if contaminated and clean models behave the same way on the permitted comparisons.

To support the at-least-80% claim, the hypothesis would need sufficient separation in the resulting rare-error observations at the stated 30% contamination level, under a rule that still respects the 5% false-positive condition.
Should “rare-error detection power” mean detecting the error pattern, or detecting contamination using that pattern?

That distinction matters. For this hypothesis to address the contamination question, power should refer to correctly flagging the specified contaminated cases *using* the rare-error signal. Merely finding that some rare errors exist would not constitute contamination detection; uncontaminated models can make rare errors too.

It would help to keep the outcome clear throughout: the observable feature is excess agreement on rare benchmark errors across paraphrases relative to twins, while the classification target is the specified paraphrase contamination. The proposed power and false-positive rates concern that classification.
How does shared reasoning challenge the hypothesis at 300 items?

Shared reasoning can create agreement across paraphrases regardless of training provenance. A model that repeatedly interprets the underlying problem the same way may reproduce the same unusual wrong answer. If a capability-matched clean model can show a similar benchmark–twin contrast, the apparent fingerprint is not specific to contamination.

The hypothesis therefore needs the twins and matched controls to distinguish the *excess* attributable to the specified exposure from this clean behavior. The item count does not remove the shared-reasoning explanation; it provides a setting in which the contrast might be assessed.
What if matched clean controls sometimes show the pattern, but not often?

The hypothesis does not require the pattern to be impossible for clean controls. A detection rule can tolerate false positives, provided its rate against the relevant uncontaminated, capability-matched controls is held to 5%. The question is whether the pattern is also common enough in the contaminated cases for the same rule to achieve at least 80% power.

Those are linked requirements. Making a rule more willing to flag modest excess agreement could raise detection power, but it could also flag more clean models. The hypothesis says a workable balance exists in the stated setting; it does not yet demonstrate that balance.
Does it matter how “rare error” is defined?

Yes. Rarity needs a reference, and the relevant one is tied to the uncontaminated, capability-matched comparison. An answer that seems unusual in isolation might be a predictable response to a recurring feature of the benchmark item. Likewise, agreement across paraphrases can seem rarer than it is if the paraphrases are treated as unrelated observations.

For the hypothesis to be interpretable, the rare-error signal should describe the pattern the detector actually uses, including its benchmark-versus-twin aspect. Otherwise the claimed 5% false-positive rate and at-least-80% power could refer to a different signal from the one being discussed.
Could the hypothesis hold for one kind of paraphrase contamination but not another, even at 30%?

Yes. The same contamination percentage does not imply the same observable effect across all possible training distributions and models. Some forms of exposure could produce a distinctive, paraphrase-stable error pattern; others might leave no such pattern, or produce behavior that a clean, capable model could also exhibit.

So the power claim needs a defined scope. It can be a hypothesis about a specified contamination regime at 30%, without becoming a claim that every regime described as 30% paraphrase contamination is detectable at 80% power.
If the twins really are exchangeable for clean models, does a benchmark-only rare-error pattern identify contamination?

Not on that assumption alone. Exchangeability constrains the clean benchmark–twin comparison, but identification also depends on what behavior the contaminated models produce and whether any allowed clean explanation can reproduce the full observed pattern. A surprising clean-model pattern may support a detection rule without uniquely revealing training provenance.

The stronger case would be one in which, under clearly stated assumptions, the specified contamination produces a benchmark-specific error contrast that the permitted shared-reasoning alternatives cannot adequately mimic. The hypothesis proposes that such a contrast is detectable at the stated power and false-positive targets in the 300-item setting; whether it exists remains to be established.
What would falsify the practical part of this hypothesis without resolving every question about contamination?

If the proposed rare-error comparison cannot attain at least 80% detection power while keeping false positives at 5% against the matched clean controls in the stated setting, the practical performance claim would not hold for that setting. That would concern this signal and comparison; it would not establish that contamination never occurred or that no other black-box signal could be useful.

Likewise, finding that clean controls exhibit the same benchmark–twin agreement pattern could undermine its use as an identifying fingerprint without settling the models' actual training histories.
What if the signal is strong for some contaminated models but absent for others?

Then an overall power figure depends on which contaminated models are included and how the figure is interpreted. A claim of at least 80% power for a defined group is different from a claim of at least 80% for each contaminated model or every possible training distribution at the 30% level.

The hypothesis should not hide that distinction behind a single percentage. Its scope determines whether models with no distinctive rare-error behavior are included in the power claim or characterized as an observationally indistinguishable regime for this comparison.
Would a clean model that matches a contaminated model on all the benchmark and twin responses be a problem even if the controls generally look different?

Yes, for any claim intended to cover that clean alternative. If their permitted black-box observations have the same distribution, a rule based on those observations cannot flag the contaminated model more often than it flags the matching clean model. A 5% false-positive limit for that clean model is incompatible with at least 80% power for the observationally identical contaminated one.

Other matched controls looking different would not eliminate that identifiability limit. It is why the assumptions defining the clean comparison matter as much as the observed contrast in a particular group of controls.
Is exchangeability something the hypothesis assumes, or something the controls would prove?

In the wording of the hypothesis, exchangeable twins are a condition under which the proposed comparison is expected to work. Matched controls can inform whether the intended comparison behaves plausibly for clean models, but their behavior alone cannot prove exchangeability across every unknown clean training distribution.

It is worth separating the assumption from the performance claim: exchangeability makes a benchmark–twin excess more interpretable, while at least 80% power at 5% false positives is the proposed detection performance. Neither should be treated as an already established experimental result.

That would leave out essential conditions. The claim is not that 300 items are universally sufficient. It is that, *at 300 items and 30% paraphrase contamination*, exchangeable twins and matched controls may enable at least 80% rare-error detection power at a 5% false-positive rate.

Suppose there is excess agreement on benchmark paraphrases but the controls sometimes show it too.

Does the plan commit us to a particular numerical power result?

Why derive identifiability regimes separately from estimating power? Doesn't one answer the other?

They answer related but distinct questions. A power estimate describes the performance of a detection rule for the contaminated and control cases within its assessed scope.
