The performance figures characterize the specified assessment, not a guarantee that every flagged response has a uniquely identifiable training history.
Can the result tell us whether adaptive black-box queries would improve power?

No. The result gives **81% power and 4.8% FPR** under its stated full-solution, shift, and mismatch conditions. It does not report a comparison of adaptive and nonadaptive querying or describe how the rates would change under a different query policy. Those would be additional claims, not implications of the two numbers.
I want to make sure the full-solution label does not get replaced with a vague reference to paraphrases.

Keep it explicit: **full-solution contamination** is the condition attached to the result. Calling it simply “paraphrase contamination” would lose the distinction the result provides, while adding a contamination percentage or an answer-only comparison would introduce details it does not report.
Give me a compact sentence with the exact values and conditions.
“Under **full-solution contamination**, TwinTrace reached **81% detection power** and **4.8% FPR** at a **two-point twin accuracy shift** and a **one-point control mismatch**.”

I’d like to propose TwinContrast: a benchmark/private-twin accuracy difference-in-differences test, calibrated on capability-matched controls, to detect answer-only contamination. What is the core comparison?

TwinContrast would compare two accuracy gaps. The first is a model’s accuracy on benchmark cases minus its accuracy on corresponding private twins. The second is the benchmark-minus-twin gap observed among uncontaminated, capability-matched controls. The difference between those gaps is the proposed detection signal.

The point is not to treat benchmark accuracy alone as evidence of answer-only contamination. It is to ask whether the benchmark/twin contrast is unusual relative to what similarly capable clean models show. This is a proposal, not a reported test result.
Why call it difference-in-differences if there’s no before-and-after measurement?

Here, the two differences are across **item sets** and across **model comparisons**, not across time. For a model being assessed, take its benchmark accuracy minus its private-twin accuracy. Then compare that gap with the corresponding gap for capability-matched clean controls. That comparison of gaps is the difference-in-differences idea.

The name does not imply that anyone has measured the model before and after training exposure, or that its training history is directly observable.
Could you write the comparison in words without assuming a particular statistic?

Yes: **How different is the assessed model’s benchmark-versus-private-twin accuracy gap from the gap expected for uncontaminated models of comparable capability?** That is the central question. A formal statistic and decision rule would have to preserve that comparison, but the proposal does not specify their exact implementation.
What does the private twin contribute that a second batch of benchmark paraphrases wouldn’t?

The private twin is intended to provide a corresponding case with the relevant task structure without being the benchmark case whose exposure is at issue. It asks whether the model’s apparent strength is specific to the benchmark side or carries over to its twin. Another paraphrase of the benchmark may still track behavior tied to benchmark-related exposure, so it does not play the same comparative role.

Privacy alone does not establish that every model lacked related training material, and the label “twin” alone does not prove equal difficulty. Those limitations affect how confidently the contrast can be interpreted.
Why is this specifically a proposal for answer-only contamination?

That is the contamination type the proposal targets. The proposed accuracy contrast asks whether exposure to benchmark answers alone can produce benchmark-specific accuracy behavior relative to private twins, beyond what capability-matched clean models show. It does not assume that such a contrast must occur, and it does not automatically extend a detection claim to other forms of contamination.

In particular, “answer-only” should stay attached to any eventual claim about this proposal rather than being silently broadened to all benchmark exposure.
If a model scores well on both benchmark items and twins, what would TwinContrast say?

High accuracy on both could be consistent with genuine generalization. What matters for TwinContrast is the *relative gap*, and whether that gap departs from the clean, capability-matched reference. Strong performance alone is not the proposed signal.

Even a small benchmark/twin gap would not prove that answer-only contamination is absent. Exposure might leave no distinctive accuracy contrast, or the resulting contrast might resemble clean-model behavior.
What if benchmark accuracy exceeds twin accuracy?

A benchmark advantage is the first difference, not yet a contamination finding. Capability-matched clean models might also have a benchmark advantage because the two sets do not elicit identical behavior. TwinContrast would ask whether the assessed model’s advantage is exceptional relative to that clean comparison.

A larger-than-expected advantage could be a candidate signal under suitable assumptions. The proposal does not assert that answer-only contamination always increases benchmark accuracy, nor that any observed advantage uniquely establishes training provenance.
Does difference-in-differences assume the controls have exactly equal benchmark and twin accuracy?

No. The control gap can be nonzero. Subtracting or otherwise comparing against it is meant to account for benchmark-versus-twin differences that occur among uncontaminated models of comparable capability.

The important assumption is not that clean controls have zero gap. It is that their benchmark/twin gap provides a valid reference for the clean behavior of the model being assessed, within the scope of the claim.
What would make that reference invalid?

If the assessed model and the capability-matched clean controls can differ in benchmark/twin accuracy gaps for reasons unrelated to answer-only contamination, the contrast may reflect those differences instead. Likewise, if private twins differ from benchmark items in task-relevant difficulty or other accuracy-relevant features, the within-model gap can be hard to attribute.

Capability matching and twin comparability are therefore substantive conditions. They are not guarantees supplied merely by the proposed test’s name.
Could capability matching be based solely on the benchmark score?

The proposal specifies **capability-matched controls** but does not prescribe a matching measure. Matching only on benchmark accuracy could be problematic for interpreting a benchmark/twin gap: the benchmark score is itself one side of the contrast being examined. Whether any proposed matching definition is adequate depends on whether it makes the clean reference relevant without building the answer-only signal into the comparison.

That is a consideration for specifying the proposal, not a statement that a particular matching approach was used.
How would the 5% false-positive requirement apply to TwinContrast?

A TwinContrast decision rule would need to flag no more than **5% of the relevant uncontaminated, capability-matched models** under the stated evaluation. Calibration on those controls is meant to make that false-positive constraint meaningful for the benchmark/twin difference-in-differences signal.

The broader objective also asks for **at least 80% detection power** against the contamination cases in scope. Neither figure is an achieved property of TwinContrast simply because the proposal specifies calibration.
Could you separate the observed accuracy contrast from the decision to flag a model?

The accuracy contrast is a behavioral quantity: the assessed model’s benchmark/twin gap relative to the corresponding clean-control gap. A positive contamination flag would be a further decision made using that quantity under a calibrated rule. The observation can exist without being large enough or distinctive enough to warrant a flag at **5% false positives**.

Even a flag is a detection decision within a specified comparison, not direct observation of training examples.
Does the difference-in-differences calculation itself control false positives?

No. It defines a comparison, not an error-rate guarantee. To claim **5% FPR**, the rule interpreting the contrast must be assessed against uncontaminated, capability-matched models within the intended scope. An accuracy gap that looks impressive without that calibration does not establish a low false-positive rate.

Likewise, controlling false positives does not ensure that answer-only contamination produces a gap often enough for **80% detection power**.
What assumption connects an exceptional accuracy contrast specifically to answer-only contamination?

The identifying assumption would have to limit how much an uncontaminated, capability-matched model can depart from the clean benchmark/twin gap through genuine generalization and other permitted variation. It would also need answer-only contamination, in the claimed regime, to produce a sufficiently distinctive contrast. Otherwise the same difference-in-differences value could have a clean explanation.

Those assumptions should be explicit because unknown training distributions do not make an accuracy contrast uniquely diagnostic of exposure.
Does using private twins make that assumption unnecessary?

No. The twins strengthen the proposed comparison by offering corresponding cases, but privacy and structural correspondence do not tell us exactly how every clean model will perform. A model may handle a benchmark case and a private twin differently without having encountered benchmark answers.

The matched controls help characterize that clean variation. The remaining inference is still conditional on the twins being comparable in the relevant sense and on the controls representing the clean alternatives against which the false-positive claim is made.
Can answer-only contamination be present with no TwinContrast signal?

Yes. Exposure need not change observable accuracy, and any change could affect benchmark items and twins similarly. Contamination might also yield a benchmark/twin gap indistinguishable from what a capability-matched clean model can produce. In those regimes, this proposed accuracy contrast cannot identify the training history.

The proposal is to test for an observable distinction, not to define answer-only contamination by the presence of that distinction.
What if a clean model has exactly the same benchmark and twin accuracy as a contaminated model?

TwinContrast would have the same accuracy information for both, so this proposed test could not distinguish them on that basis. The models might still differ in other black-box behavior; equality of two accuracy summaries is weaker than full behavioral equivalence.

If they are equivalent across *all* observations a permitted black-box evaluation can use, the limit is stronger: no such evaluation can identify which of the two training histories occurred.
Would collecting more private twins fix a lack of identifiability?

More relevant observations could help if answer-only contamination and genuine generalization produce distinguishable accuracy behavior that the current comparison has not captured reliably. But additional twins cannot establish provenance when contaminated and clean alternatives remain behaviorally identical across the permitted observations.

The proposal does not specify a number of twins or promise that expanding the comparison will yield the required detection power.
Does TwinContrast depend on rare-error agreement across paraphrases?

Its defining signal here is an **accuracy difference-in-differences** between benchmark items and private twins, calibrated on capability-matched controls. The proposal does not require a rare-error fingerprint as its detection statistic. Correct and incorrect responses contribute to accuracy, but an accuracy contrast does not, by itself, specify which particular errors recur across paraphrases.

The inference question remains the same: whether the observable contrast distinguishes answer-only contamination from clean, comparably capable generalization under explicit assumptions.
How should I phrase the identifiability limit for this particular proposal?

If an answer-only-contaminated model and an admissible uncontaminated, capability-matched model yield the same benchmark/private-twin accuracy contrast, **TwinContrast cannot distinguish them using that contrast**. If they yield the same distribution over all permitted black-box interactions, no black-box detector can distinguish their histories at all.

Keeping those two scopes separate avoids turning a limitation of an accuracy-based proposal into an unwarranted claim about every possible black-box observation.
Can this proposal be said to meet the 80%-power target already?

No. TwinContrast is a proposed test, not a reported evaluation result. To claim at least **80% detection power at 5% false positives**, one would need evidence for the specified answer-only contamination cases and the relevant uncontaminated, capability-matched controls. The proposal states what to compare and how to calibrate the comparison; it does not supply those performance figures.
What would the most careful one-sentence statement of TwinContrast be?

“**TwinContrast is a proposed benchmark/private-twin accuracy difference-in-differences test, calibrated against capability-matched clean controls, for detecting answer-only contamination.**” That states the target, comparison, and calibration without claiming that an accuracy gap is inherently diagnostic or that a power target has already been reached.
Can TwinContrast identify answer-only contamination when unknown training distributions induce baseline benchmark–twin accuracy gaps among clean models?

Possibly, but a baseline gap makes the answer conditional. TwinContrast compares an assessed model’s benchmark-minus-private-twin accuracy gap with the corresponding gap among capability-matched clean models. A nonzero gap among clean models is not itself a problem: the difference-in-differences comparison is intended to account for it.

The difficulty is that unknown training distributions may produce *different* baseline gaps for different clean models. If the assessed model’s gap could arise through genuine generalization in an admissible clean model, an excess relative to selected controls does not, by itself, identify answer-only contamination.
So the test needn’t assume clean models have equal accuracy on benchmarks and twins?

Correct. It need not assume the clean benchmark–twin gap is zero. It needs a defensible account of the gap that clean, capability-matched models can have—and of how that gap varies across the clean models covered by the claim.

Subtracting a clean reference gap addresses a common baseline difference. It does not automatically remove variation in baseline gaps arising from unknown training distributions.
Could you describe the comparison more precisely?

Call a model’s benchmark accuracy minus its private-twin accuracy its *gap*. TwinContrast asks whether the assessed model’s gap departs from the gap expected under the relevant uncontaminated, capability-matched comparison. That departure is the proposed signal.

There are two inferential steps. One is measuring the departure. The other is deciding whether it is distinctive of answer-only contamination rather than a gap that a clean model could produce. The arithmetic supplies the first step, not the second.
What if all the clean controls have a benchmark advantage?

Then a benchmark advantage in the assessed model is not distinctive merely because it is positive. The relevant question is whether its advantage differs from the *range and pattern* of advantages available to clean, capability-matched models under the assumptions being used.

The test can accommodate a clean benchmark advantage in principle. What it cannot do without further justification is assume that the particular clean controls reveal every baseline gap possible under the unknown training distributions.
Is matching overall capability enough to justify using their gaps as the baseline?

Not necessarily. Two models can be comparable in general capability yet differ in how that capability transfers between benchmark items and private twins. If those differences can arise without answer-only contamination, capability matching alone does not make their gaps interchangeable.

For the contrast to support identification, the clean controls must adequately constrain the benchmark–twin gaps of the clean alternatives to which the conclusion is meant to apply. That is an assumption about the comparison, not a consequence of the phrase “capability-matched.”
How can unknown training distributions matter if the evaluation is entirely black-box?

They matter because the evaluation tries to infer a hidden cause from observed accuracy. Different uncontaminated training distributions might lead to different benchmark–twin gaps, even when models are similarly capable. The evaluator observes the gap but not the training distribution that produced it.

TwinContrast must therefore distinguish an effect attributed to answer-only contamination from the baseline variation allowed among clean models. If those effects overlap in the permitted observations, black-box accuracy cannot by itself determine which cause applies.
Does the word “private” ensure clean models won’t have such gaps?

No. Private twins are intended as corresponding comparison cases, not as a guarantee of equal accuracy. A clean model could answer benchmark items and private twins differently through generalization or through differences in how the cases elicit its capabilities.

Privacy does not reveal the model’s unknown training distribution, and it does not by itself bound the clean benchmark–twin gap. The value of the twins depends on whether they make the contrast interpretable under the stated clean alternatives.
If a model’s gap exceeds the average gap of the controls, isn't that evidence?

It is an observed departure from that average. Whether it is evidence *specific to contamination* depends on the variation among admissible clean models. An average can conceal clean models with substantially different gaps. A model can be above the control average and still have a gap compatible with genuine generalization.

A calibrated decision needs to address how unusual the departure is under the clean comparison, not simply whether it lies above a mean. Even a departure judged unusual relative to chosen controls remains conditional on those controls representing the clean alternatives in scope.
What if the controls’ gaps vary widely?

Wide clean variation makes it harder to attribute a particular gap to answer-only contamination. The contaminated cases would need to produce a contrast sufficiently distinguishable from that variation for TwinContrast to discriminate while limiting false flags on clean models.

It would be inappropriate to declare identification merely because the assessed model has a large gap in absolute terms. What counts is its separation from the allowed clean gaps, including variation associated with unknown training distributions.
And if the controls’ gaps vary very little?

That can make a departure more informative *for the clean models those controls adequately represent*. It does not establish that every uncontaminated, capability-matched model under an unknown training distribution has a similarly narrow gap.

The conclusion should be as broad as the justified clean comparison and no broader. Narrow variation in observed controls helps only if admissible clean alternatives outside that narrow behavior have been appropriately addressed.
Is the needed assumption just that contamination increases benchmark accuracy?

No. Even if answer-only contamination increases benchmark accuracy in some cases, a clean model could also have higher benchmark than twin accuracy. Nor does an accuracy increase alone say how the benchmark–twin *gap* compares with the clean baseline.

An identifying assumption must concern the observable contrast: the specified contamination produces a gap, or a distribution of gaps, that the admitted clean explanations cannot adequately reproduce. The effect’s direction and its distinction from clean baseline variation both matter.
Does difference-in-differences remove any benchmark–twin difficulty difference?

It can account for a difficulty difference that manifests comparably in the assessed model and the clean controls. It does not automatically cancel a difference whose effect varies among models. If a clean model responds differently to the benchmark/twin comparison than the chosen controls do, subtraction can leave a residual that looks like a contamination signal.

Thus the analogy to difference-in-differences carries a comparison assumption: the clean reference must say something reliable about the assessed model’s gap *in the absence of answer-only contamination*. That counterfactual gap is not directly observed.
Could two clean models have the same overall capability and different counterfactual gaps?

Yes, that is exactly the possibility the question raises. Comparable capability need not determine accuracy on each of two distinct sets of cases, or determine their difference. The unknown training distributions can leave room for distinct clean benchmark–twin gaps.

If that room includes the observed gap of an answer-only-contaminated model, accuracy difference-in-differences may not identify which training history produced the observation.
When would a nonzero clean baseline still permit identification?

When the baseline is sufficiently constrained for the intended clean class and the specified answer-only contamination produces an observable departure that class cannot plausibly mimic at the claimed error rates. A clean gap can be nonzero and still be a useful reference if its allowable variation is understood.

That is a conditional statement about identifiability, not a claim that TwinContrast has already established the necessary constraint or separation.
Do the controls have to predict the exact gap for every clean model?

Not necessarily. A detection rule can allow clean gaps to vary; it needs the probability of flagging an admitted clean model to remain within its stated false-positive constraint. Exact prediction of every individual gap would be stronger than that requirement.

For a broad guarantee, however, the allowed clean variation must still be bounded or characterized sufficiently to justify that error rate. If arbitrary clean gaps are admitted, an extreme gap cannot be taken as uniquely attributable to contamination.
Suppose the contaminated and clean gap distributions overlap. Does that mean TwinContrast is useless?

Not necessarily. Overlap can make individual attribution uncertain without eliminating every possibility of discrimination. Whether a useful detection rule exists depends on the extent of overlap and the error rates required.

The stronger impossibility case is when the permitted TwinContrast observations have the *same distribution* under an answer-only-contaminated model and an admissible clean model. Then a rule using those observations must flag both with the same probability. Partial overlap, by contrast, limits what can be claimed but does not alone settle achievable power.
If their accuracy gaps are equal, are their training histories observationally indistinguishable?

They are indistinguishable **to a rule using only that gap**, provided its other relevant observations do not differ. Equal aggregate gaps do not imply identical answers to individual items, identical response variability, or equality across every possible black-box interaction.

A general black-box impossibility claim requires behavioral equivalence across all permitted observations. TwinContrast has a narrower limitation whenever the particular accuracy contrast it uses cannot separate the alternatives.
Can looking at benchmark and twin accuracies separately rescue two models with the same gap?

It might reveal that the component accuracies differ despite an equal gap. Whether that helps identify contamination would still require a clean comparison and assumptions connecting those observations to answer-only exposure. Equal gaps alone do not establish equality of all accuracy information.

Conversely, even matching component accuracies would not prove full behavioral equivalence: aggregate accuracy leaves many response patterns unspecified. The scope of any identification or impossibility statement must match the observations actually used.
What if the assessed model has a bigger gap because its twin accuracy is lower, rather than because its benchmark accuracy is higher?

The same arithmetic gap can arise in different ways. TwinContrast’s gap alone does not establish which component changed relative to a counterfactual clean version of that model, much less why it changed. A lower twin accuracy could affect the contrast without demonstrating exposure to benchmark answers.

This is another reason to distinguish a measured difference-in-differences from a causal attribution. The proposed detection claim depends on what component behavior clean, capability-matched models are allowed to exhibit.
Does a baseline gap among clean models undermine the false-positive calibration?

Not merely by being nonzero. Calibration can include the clean models’ benchmark–twin gaps. The concern is *mismatch*: if other uncontaminated, capability-matched models have a different distribution of gaps from the controls used for calibration, the false-positive rate observed or stipulated for those controls need not carry over.

The appropriate question is whether the calibration covers the clean variation permitted by the claim, including variation induced by unknown training distributions.
Could I calibrate to the most unusual clean gap and then identify anything beyond it?

A boundary observed among selected controls is not automatically the outer boundary for all admissible clean models. Whether a gap beyond it warrants a flag depends on how controls are related to the intended clean class, how uncertainty is handled, and what decision rule is being claimed.

Nor does a clean boundary alone establish detection power: answer-only contamination must yield departures often enough for the test to be useful. The question remains about two distributions of observable behavior, not just one striking assessed gap.
How would I state the identifiability assumption without assuming every clean training distribution is known?

You can state a condition on the *observable consequences* of the admissible clean distributions. For example, the clean, capability-matched models covered by the claim must have benchmark/private-twin gap behavior sufficiently constrained by the control comparison that the specified contaminated behavior remains distinguishable at the desired error rates.

That does not require listing every training example. It does require saying which clean alternatives are admitted and not treating unobserved clean baseline variation as though it cannot exist.
So the difference-in-differences approach isn't a causal guarantee by itself?

Exactly. The calculation removes the clean reference gap as defined by the controls. For that subtraction to isolate an effect of answer-only contamination, the controls must represent what the assessed model’s benchmark–twin gap could have been without the contamination, within the intended scope. Unknown training distributions make that an assumption to justify, not a fact supplied by the formula.

Without it, a residual gap can be an informative behavioral observation while remaining ambiguous as to training provenance.
Can you give a careful direct answer to my original question?

**Yes, conditionally.** TwinContrast can distinguish answer-only contamination despite nonzero clean benchmark–twin accuracy gaps if capability-matched controls adequately constrain those baseline gaps and the contaminated models produce a distinguishable excess gap. **No unconditional identification follows** when unknown clean training distributions can produce the same relevant accuracy contrast—or the same full permitted black-box behavior—as the contaminated alternatives.

A baseline gap is something the difference-in-differences comparison can account for; uncontrolled variation in that gap is the identifiability problem.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: if the controls bound benchmark–twin gap drift to one point, TwinContrast achieves at least 80% detection power at a 5% false-positive rate under 30% answer-only contamination. How does that address the uncertainty in clean models’ baseline gaps?

It makes control of the **clean benchmark–twin accuracy gap** an explicit condition of the performance claim. TwinContrast compares a model’s benchmark-versus-private-twin accuracy gap with the gap of capability-matched clean controls. If those controls bound how far the relevant clean baseline gap can drift to **one point**, the hypothesis is that the remaining contrast is informative enough to detect **30% answer-only contamination** with **at least 80% power at 5% FPR**.

This is a hypothesis, not a deduction from the one-point bound alone. The contaminated models must also produce sufficiently distinguishable accuracy behavior.
What exactly would be drifting by one point?

The quantity is the **benchmark-minus-twin accuracy gap among clean models**, relative to the gap used as TwinContrast’s clean reference. “One point” should be understood as a bound on that gap’s drift, not as a one-point bound on either benchmark accuracy or twin accuracy taken separately.

The hypothesis does not specify the precise reference, the direction of drift, or how the bound is established. Those would need to be clear before treating it as a testable guarantee.
Does a one-point gap-drift bound mean clean models’ benchmark and twin accuracies are within one point of each other?

No. A clean model could have a nonzero benchmark–twin gap. The proposed bound concerns how much that **gap changes relative to the clean reference**, not whether the gap itself is zero or at most one point.

For example, the conceptual distinction is between the *level* of a clean gap and the *variation* in that gap across the clean comparison. The hypothesis constrains the latter; it does not assign a value to the former.
Does “one point” mean a one-percentage-point increase in TwinContrast’s false-positive rate?

No. It describes drift in an **accuracy gap**. The **5% FPR** is a separate measure: how often uncontaminated models are flagged as contaminated. A one-point change in an accuracy gap does not automatically translate into a one-percentage-point change in FPR.

The hypothesis asserts that TwinContrast can retain the stated detection performance when gap drift is bounded. Establishing that assertion requires connecting the gap behavior to the rule’s clean-model flags.
If the controls bound clean drift, why isn't the 5% false-positive rate automatic?

Because the size of a gap-drift bound does not itself specify TwinContrast’s decision rule or how close clean models can come to its flagging boundary. A one-point change might be inconsequential for one rule but matter for another. Also, bounding a particular accuracy summary does not necessarily bound every other observable difference that affects a decision.

Calibration at **5% FPR** is therefore part of the claim to assess. It does not follow just from writing “one point” next to the controls.
What is the role of capability matching in this conditional claim?

The controls need to be relevant clean comparators for the assessed models, rather than models whose benchmark–twin gaps differ simply because of broad capability differences. Capability matching supports that comparison. The additional **one-point gap-drift bound** addresses a more specific problem: comparably capable clean models may still have different benchmark–twin gaps under unknown training distributions.

Neither property alone proves that answer-only contamination is identifiable. The hypothesis combines a constrained clean reference with a proposed performance outcome.
Could the controls themselves have a sizable benchmark advantage and still satisfy the hypothesis?

Yes. A sizable **baseline** benchmark advantage is different from substantial **drift** in that advantage across the clean models the controls are meant to cover. TwinContrast compares the assessed gap to the clean reference gap, so the latter need not be zero.

What matters for the hypothesis is whether clean baseline variation is bounded to one point in the intended sense and whether the 30%-contaminated condition produces a sufficiently detectable departure from that clean behavior.
Does the one-point bound refer to every clean model or just to an average?

That scope needs to be stated. A bound on the **average** clean gap would not ensure that each uncontaminated, capability-matched model has a gap near the control reference. A bound applying to **every admitted clean alternative** is a stronger condition.

The scope matters particularly if the **5% FPR** claim is intended for clean models beyond the particular controls. The hypothesis’s wording identifies a one-point bound but does not, by itself, resolve whether that bound is individual, distributional, or limited to a specified control population.
What does “30% answer-only contamination” tell us about the accuracy contrast?

It specifies the contamination condition for the proposed **power** claim. It does not tell us how many answers change, whether benchmark accuracy rises, or how large the benchmark–twin gap becomes. In particular, **30% contamination** is not a prediction of a 30-point gap or an 80% detection rate.

The hypothesized result is that TwinContrast detects that condition with **at least 80% power** while operating at **5% FPR**. The observable effect required for that performance remains something to establish.
Should I interpret 80% power as identifying 80% of the contaminated benchmark items?

No. **Power** concerns how often the test flags the specified contaminated condition, not a reported fraction of individual benchmark items identified. The hypothesis supplies no item-level detection count or allocation of contamination across items.

Likewise, the **5% FPR** concerns positive flags for uncontaminated models in the relevant clean comparison, not a fraction of benchmark items that are wrong.
Does the condition cover all types of answer-only contamination?

Not without specifying that broad scope and showing the required separation for it. Different cases described as **30% answer-only contamination** could have different observable effects. Some could leave a benchmark–twin accuracy gap that clean models can reproduce.

The hypothesis can be read as a performance claim for a defined answer-only contamination regime under the one-point clean-gap condition. It should not silently become a guarantee for every unknown training distribution with a 30% label.
If clean gap drift is within one point, couldn't contaminated and clean models still have the same gap?

Yes. A bound on variation among **clean** gaps does not force a contaminated model’s gap to lie outside that range. If the contaminated and clean alternatives have the same TwinContrast accuracy observations, that contrast cannot distinguish their histories, regardless of how tightly the clean gaps are bounded.

That is why the one-point condition is not sufficient on its own. The proposed **≥80% power at 5% FPR** also requires an observable separation for the contaminated cases in scope.
Could TwinContrast still be informative if the two gap distributions overlap?

Potentially. Some overlap does not rule out a useful decision rule. The question is whether the contaminated distribution puts enough probability on outcomes that are sufficiently uncommon under the admitted clean comparison to reach **at least 80% power** while keeping **FPR at 5%**.

If the distributions of all observations TwinContrast uses are identical, however, no such rule can attain those two rates for that pair of alternatives. A one-point clean-drift bound does not remove that impossibility.
What if the gap differs by more than one point from the control gap? Is that automatically a contamination flag?

No. The one-point figure is a proposed **bound on clean baseline drift**, not a stated TwinContrast decision threshold. An observed departure might be relevant, but issuing a flag also depends on the calibrated rule, uncertainty in the comparison, and which clean alternatives it covers.

Nor does crossing one point prove that answer-only contamination caused the departure. The hypothesis proposes performance for a particular comparison; it does not equate a numerical gap with direct observation of training provenance.
Could a contaminated model be flagged because its twin accuracy falls rather than because its benchmark accuracy rises?

A benchmark-minus-twin gap could widen in either way. The gap alone does not reveal what an otherwise identical model would have scored without contamination, so it cannot by itself assign the change to benchmark exposure or to a particular component of accuracy.

The hypothesis is about TwinContrast’s **detection performance**, conditional on the controls bounding clean gap drift. It does not specify a mechanism by which 30% answer-only contamination changes benchmark or twin accuracy.
Do I need a reason the controls' one-point bound transfers to other clean models?

Yes, if the 5% false-positive claim is meant to cover those other models. Observing or imposing a bound for selected controls is not the same as bounding all uncontaminated, capability-matched models under unknown training distributions. A clean model outside the control comparison could have a different gap for reasons unrelated to contamination.

The identifiability assumption must say which clean models the controls constrain. Otherwise the conditional claim may hold for the controls used for calibration without justifying the same FPR for a wider clean class.
Is the one-point bound meant to solve twin comparability too?

It helps constrain the **resulting clean benchmark–twin accuracy gap**, which is directly relevant to TwinContrast. It does not by itself explain *why* benchmark items and private twins differ or certify that they are equivalent in every task-relevant respect. Two paired sets might have a stable baseline gap that the controls capture; the difference-in-differences comparison can use that reference without requiring zero difference.

The essential condition is that the controls bound the clean gap variation relevant to the assessed model. Treating a numerical drift limit as a blanket certificate of twin comparability would overstate it.
Would the hypothesis be met if power were exactly 80% and FPR exactly 5%?

Yes. **At least 80%** includes exactly 80% power, and a claim of performance **at 5% FPR** uses that false-positive operating condition. Higher power at the same stated FPR would also satisfy the power requirement.

Those are interpretations of the proposed thresholds, not findings that TwinContrast reaches them.
Could the test reach 80% power by accepting more than 5% false positives?

It might reach a power figure under a different operating condition, but that would **not** establish this hypothesis. The proposed performance is **≥80% power at 5% FPR**, not power considered independently of clean-model errors.

The clean-gap-drift condition matters because the false-positive claim must remain meaningful for the capability-matched clean comparison despite variation in baseline benchmark–twin accuracy gaps.
Does the hypothesis say TwinContrast reaches that power throughout contamination levels from zero to 30%?

No. It says **under 30% answer-only contamination**. That is a condition for the power claim, not a promise of the same power at all lower contamination levels. The one-point figure concerns **clean benchmark–twin gap drift**, not a range of contamination percentages.
What would observing less than 80% power tell us, without making a claim about every black-box method?

If the relevant assessment found TwinContrast below **80% power at 5% FPR** under the specified **30% answer-only** condition and a properly established **one-point clean-gap-drift bound**, it would fail the performance claim for that assessed setting. Is it fair to describe 5% FPR as a universal guarantee for all uncontaminated language models?

No. The reported rate is tied to the relevant clean comparison under the **one-point benchmark–twin gap-drift condition**. It does not establish the same false-positive rate for every uncontaminated model under every unknown training distribution. A clean model whose gap behavior falls outside the comparison’s assumptions is not automatically covered by this figure.
Does the result establish what happens with fewer or more than 500 pairs?

No. It reports performance **with 500 pairs**. It does not supply a relationship between pair count and power, or a performance figure for any other number of pairs. The stated count is a condition of this result, not a general formula for how TwinContrast scales.
Can I infer performance at another amount of clean-model gap drift?

Not from this figure. The result is conditioned on **one-point clean-model gap drift**. It does not report power or FPR at zero drift, at greater drift, or throughout a range of drift values. Describing 85% as holding whenever drift is *at most* one point would extend the claim beyond the stated condition unless that range were separately established.
And does it establish power at contamination levels other than 30%?

No. **30% answer-only contamination** is the specified contaminated condition. The **85%** figure is not a power curve across contamination levels and does not determine performance at a smaller or larger percentage.
If answer-only contamination and a clean model happened to give the same accuracy contrast, would this result still identify which model was contaminated?

The accuracy contrast alone could not distinguish two models that produce the same TwinContrast observations. That limitation is compatible with an aggregate power result for the specified assessed conditions: **85% power** does not mean every possible contaminated model has a unique accuracy signature.

If a contaminated and clean alternative are identical across all permitted black-box observations, no black-box decision can distinguish their training histories. This result does not claim that such alternatives are excluded from every possible training distribution.
Could the 85% be explained as a particular increase in benchmark accuracy?

The result does not provide such a breakdown. It reports TwinContrast’s detection power and FPR, not the separate benchmark and private-twin accuracies or a measured increase in either one. Assigning the detection figure to a particular accuracy change or causal mechanism would add information that is not stated.
How should I keep the 5% FPR and the one-point gap drift from being conflated?

Describe them in their separate roles: **one-point clean-model gap drift** is a condition on variation in the clean benchmark–twin accuracy comparison; **5% FPR** is the reported rate of positive flags in the clean comparison. The first constrains the setting in which TwinContrast is assessed. The second describes its classification performance at that operating point.
Give me one concise sentence that reports only what this finding establishes.
“With **500 benchmark/private-twin pairs** and **one-point clean-model benchmark–twin gap drift**, TwinContrast reached **85% detection power at 5% FPR** under **30% answer-only contamination**.”
When can contamination-induced benchmark–twin accuracy gaps be replicated by clean models under unknown training distributions, regardless of sample size?

They can be replicated when the admitted **uncontaminated, capability-matched models** can produce the same benchmark/private-twin accuracy contrast through genuine generalization or other clean training histories. TwinContrast observes an accuracy difference-in-differences; it does not observe the cause of that difference. If a clean alternative produces the same distribution of the observations TwinContrast uses as a contaminated alternative, increasing the number of pairs cannot distinguish their histories using TwinContrast.

The phrase “regardless of sample size” needs that qualification. An equal-looking gap in one finite assessment is not necessarily an impossibility. The impossibility arises when the alternatives remain observationally equivalent for the comparison even with additional permitted observations.
What does a clean model have to replicate—the contaminated model’s benchmark accuracy, its twin accuracy, or just their difference?

That depends on what the detector is allowed to use. If TwinContrast uses only the **benchmark-minus-twin accuracy gap relative to a clean-control gap**, a clean model that reproduces the distribution of that statistic defeats identification *from that statistic*. It need not match every underlying answer.

If the evaluation also uses benchmark and twin accuracies separately, or individual responses, matching the gap alone may not suffice. A claim that **no black-box evaluation** can distinguish the histories requires equality across all permitted observations, not merely equality of one aggregate gap.
So an identical difference-in-differences value is not automatically full behavioral equivalence?

Correct. Two models can have the same difference-in-differences value while differing on which items they answer correctly, how they respond to paraphrases, or other permitted queries. That equal value limits what the *gap-based comparison* can establish; it does not prove the models are indistinguishable to every possible black-box test.

Conversely, if a clean and contaminated model have the same distribution over every permitted black-box interaction, their accuracy gaps necessarily provide no distinction either.
How could a clean model produce a benchmark advantage without having seen benchmark answers?

Conceptually, it could generalize in a way that works better on the benchmark cases than on their private twins. The cases may elicit different responses even if they are intended to test corresponding abilities, and comparable overall capability does not require an identical benchmark–twin gap for every clean model.

That is a possible alternative explanation under unknown training distributions, not a claim that it occurs in any particular comparison. The identifiability question is whether the allowed clean alternatives include models whose gaps reproduce the purported contamination signal.
If the private twins are genuinely isomorphic, doesn't that prevent a clean benchmark advantage?

Not by itself. Task-structural correspondence makes the comparison more meaningful, but distinct inputs need not elicit identical accuracy from a black-box model. To rule out a clean advantage, an assumption must constrain the **accuracy-gap behavior** of uncontaminated, capability-matched models—not merely describe the twins as isomorphic.

A nonzero clean baseline gap can also be incorporated into TwinContrast’s difference-in-differences reference. The harder issue is whether unknown clean training distributions permit *variation* in that gap that resembles the proposed contamination effect.
Where do capability-matched controls help, and where do they stop helping?

They establish a relevant clean reference for the benchmark–twin comparison and for controlling false positives. They help prevent a general difference in competence from being mistaken for an exposure signal.

They stop short of proving that every admissible clean model has the same gap distribution as the controls. If an unknown clean training distribution can yield a capability-matched model with a contamination-like gap outside the behavior represented by those controls, calibration on the selected controls alone does not identify provenance for that broader clean class.
Is this mainly a question about a baseline gap being nonzero?

No. A *known or adequately constrained* nonzero baseline is compatible with a useful difference-in-differences comparison: TwinContrast compares against that baseline rather than assuming it is zero. The problem is an **unconstrained or insufficiently constrained clean baseline**. If the admissible clean gaps can take the same values, with the same relevant distribution, as contaminated gaps, the residual contrast cannot uniquely indicate contamination.

Thus the issue is not whether clean models ever favor benchmark items. It is whether the proposed contamination-induced departure is distinguishable from the clean departures permitted by the unknown training distributions.
What if contaminated and clean models have the same average gap, but their gaps vary differently?

Then equality of averages alone does not establish an impossibility. If the evaluation can observe and use a difference in the *distribution* of gaps or in the responses behind them, it may have a basis for discrimination. Whether it can do so at a specified false-positive rate and useful power is a further question.

For a sample-size-independent impossibility for a given detector, the clean alternative must match the distribution of the detector’s permitted observations sufficiently completely, not just match one expected accuracy gap.
Suppose the contaminated and clean distributions of the TwinContrast statistic are exactly the same. What follows at 5% false positives?

Any rule that flags contamination using that statistic has the **same probability of flagging** under both distributions. If the rule is constrained to flag the clean alternative at most **5%** of the time, its detection power against the matching contaminated alternative is at most **5%**. It cannot reach **80% power at 5% false positives** for that pair using the identical statistic distribution.

This conclusion does not depend on the number of benchmark/private-twin pairs. Adding pairs does not help if the clean alternative can continue to match the complete distribution of the statistic the rule observes.
Why do you say “can continue to match”? Couldn't more pairs reveal a difference?

They could if the original match was only a coincidence of limited sampling or held only for a particular finite set of pairs. More pairs may reveal a real difference between the alternatives’ observable distributions.

“Regardless of sample size” applies to a stronger condition: within the class of pairs and interactions the evaluation is permitted to use, the clean and contaminated alternatives produce the same relevant observation distribution for each allowed assessment. It is that continuing observational equivalence—not merely a matching estimate at one sample size—that makes additional pairs uninformative about which history occurred.
What if the distributions differ, but the difference becomes arbitrarily small for some clean models?

Then exact impossibility need not hold for each fixed pair, but a **uniform** performance claim across the whole admitted class can still fail. For any proposed amount of evidence, an allowed clean alternative might be so close in the permitted observations to a contaminated one that a rule controlling false positives cannot attain the desired power for that pair.

That is distinct from saying no pair is ever distinguishable with enough observations. The scope matters: power against a specified, separated contamination regime is a different claim from power against every regime allowed by unrestricted unknown training distributions.
Can you relate that to total variation without assuming a particular TwinContrast implementation?

For any fixed decision event, the difference between its flagging probability under contaminated and clean observation distributions cannot exceed their **total-variation distance**. To obtain **80% power** while holding false positives to **5%** for a given pair, that distance must be at least **0.75** over the complete observations available to that decision.

That is a necessary separation condition for the given assessment, not a claim that TwinContrast has that separation. When discussing additional pairs, the relevant distance is between distributions of the *entire enlarged observation*, not just between single-pair accuracy gaps.
Could every clean training distribution be unknown while the test is still identifiable?

Yes, if the admitted clean alternatives have sufficiently constrained **observable benchmark–twin behavior**, even though their underlying training distributions are not known in detail. Identification does not require reconstructing every training example; it requires an observable distinction between the specified contaminated class and the permitted clean class.

If the assumptions leave clean benchmark–twin gaps free to reproduce the contaminated gap distribution, however, the unknown training distributions preserve an alternative explanation that TwinContrast cannot eliminate through sample size alone.
Would a bound on clean gap drift resolve this?

It can help by restricting which clean accuracy contrasts are admissible. But a bound on clean drift is not sufficient by itself: contaminated models must also produce a distinguishable distribution of TwinContrast observations. If their gaps fall within behavior that an admitted clean model can reproduce, a tight clean bound does not force identification.

The bound must also apply to the clean models covered by the false-positive claim, rather than only to a selected set of controls. Otherwise an unrepresented clean alternative could still replicate the signal.
Does a matching clean gap prove that the contamination had no effect?

No. A contaminated model might have a gap that was affected by exposure yet happens to match a gap produced by a clean model for another reason. Black-box equality of the resulting contrast does not reveal the contaminated model’s unobserved counterfactual performance without exposure.

The point is epistemic: the **same observed gap can have different causes**. TwinContrast cannot assign the cause uniquely when its permitted observations fail to separate those alternatives.
Could the component accuracies provide evidence even when the difference-in-differences matches?

Potentially. The same difference can arise from different benchmark and twin accuracy levels. If those component accuracies are available to a detector and differ between the alternatives, they supply observations beyond the single difference-in-differences value.

They still do not automatically identify answer-only contamination. Clean models under unknown training distributions may reproduce the component accuracies too. Each stronger claim about indistinguishability must cover the additional observations it allows the evaluator to use.
What if we observe each model on an unlimited supply of private twins?

An unlimited supply could remove sampling uncertainty about differences that actually exist on those permitted comparisons. It cannot reveal training provenance when an admissible clean model generates the same distribution of responses on the entire supply as the contaminated model.

If the two models differ on some twins or benchmark cases, additional observations might expose that difference. The phrase “regardless of sample size” should therefore be reserved for equivalence that persists over the relevant observation process, not for every case in which a finite accuracy estimate is inconclusive.
Does the answer change if the evaluator chooses queries adaptively?

Adaptation may help if it can elicit a behavioral difference that the original pairs or aggregate gap missed. But if the clean and contaminated alternatives give the same conditional response distribution after every permitted query-and-response history, they generate the same distribution of adaptive transcripts. No adaptive rule can then distinguish their training histories.

Equivalence of one fixed TwinContrast gap is weaker than that adaptive behavioral-equivalence premise. The scope of the impossibility must match the queries and observations actually permitted.
How should I distinguish a contaminated model being hard to detect from contamination being unidentifiable?

“Hard to detect” can mean the relevant distributions differ but overlap substantially, or that the available assessment does not estimate their difference reliably. “Unidentifiable from the permitted observations” means a clean and contaminated alternative can generate the **same observation distribution**, so no rule based on those observations can assign different detection probabilities to them.

A failure to obtain a striking accuracy gap in a finite sample establishes neither exact equivalence nor a universal impossibility. Conversely, constructing an observationally equivalent clean alternative gives an impossibility within the defined observation scope regardless of sample size.
If a clean model matches the contaminated gap but not the contaminated model's individual answers, does that defeat TwinContrast?

It defeats identification **if TwinContrast’s decision uses only that matched gap distribution**. A detector allowed to examine individual answers might find a distinction, but that would require its own calibrated clean comparison and would be a broader observation set than the matched accuracy summary.

So there are two levels to state carefully: replication of the TwinContrast signal limits TwinContrast; replication of every permitted black-box observation limits any evaluation restricted to those observations.
Can baseline gap variation produce false positives even if the private twins are well constructed?

Yes, in principle. Well-constructed private twins address the comparability of the paired cases, but capability-matched clean models may still vary in how they perform across those cases. If the controls used to calibrate TwinContrast do not cover that permissible clean variation, an uncontaminated model’s gap could look like the proposed answer-only-contamination signal.

Whether the false-positive rate actually exceeds a stated limit is an empirical question for the specified comparison. The identifiability concern is that twin construction alone does not rule out clean replication of the gap.
Would observing the same gap repeatedly make contamination more identifiable?

Repeated observations can establish that the gap is stable rather than a sampling fluctuation. They cannot establish its cause if an admissible clean model can stably reproduce the same distribution. With sufficient observations, one might know the behavioral contrast very precisely and still not know whether answer-only contamination or genuine generalization produced it.

That is the distinction between **precision about behavior** and **identification of training history**.
What assumption would exclude that clean replication without pretending we know all training distributions?

One would need to constrain the permitted **clean observable gap distributions**: for example, specify that uncontaminated, capability-matched models covered by the claim cannot produce the contaminated regime’s relevant benchmark/private-twin contrast at the stated false-positive frequency. The assumption must be justified for the intended class of clean alternatives, not just asserted from the existence of controls.

The contaminated regime also needs a specified observable effect. Restricting clean drift does not help if the contaminated observations remain inside the allowed clean distribution.
Does TwinContrast's calibration by itself supply that assumption?

No. Calibration describes how a positive accuracy contrast is judged against selected capability-matched clean controls. The identifiability assumption concerns whether those controls constrain *all clean alternatives admitted by the claim* under unknown training distributions.

A well-calibrated rule for one clean comparison can still misattribute a gap if a different admissible clean model reproduces the contaminated signal. Calibration and coverage of the clean class are related but distinct requirements.
Can you answer the original “when” question in one careful statement?

Contamination-induced benchmark–twin accuracy gaps can be replicated by clean models, **regardless of sample size**, when the unknown but admissible clean training distributions permit uncontaminated, capability-matched models to generate the **same distribution of TwinContrast observations** as the contaminated models for every allowed amount of paired evaluation. In that regime, the accuracy contrast identifies behavior but not its training cause; at **5% false positives**, an observationally identical contaminated alternative can be detected with no more than **5% power** using that contrast.

Matching only a finite-sample gap or its average is a weaker statement. More pairs may distinguish alternatives that truly differ; they cannot distinguish histories whose permitted black-box observations remain behaviorally identical.

I want to state the identifiability hypothesis this way: if clean training reproduces the contaminated benchmark–twin accuracy gaps and all adaptive response distributions, no black-box test can have detection power exceeding its false-positive rate. Is that the right conditional claim?

Yes, provided “all adaptive response distributions” covers every interaction the black-box test is permitted to conduct. The hypothesis is conditional: it does **not** assert that a particular clean training distribution actually reproduces a particular contaminated model. It says what follows **if** an admissible clean alternative matches both the benchmark–twin gaps and the complete observable behavior under adaptive querying.

Under that condition, a test sees identically distributed evidence whether the model is contaminated or clean. Its probability of flagging contamination—its power under the contaminated alternative—must equal its probability of flagging the clean alternative, which is its false-positive rate for that comparison. It therefore cannot exceed that rate.
Why mention the benchmark–twin gaps if matching every adaptive response distribution already sounds stronger?

The gaps identify the particular signal at issue for TwinContrast: benchmark accuracy relative to private-twin accuracy. Matching those gaps explains why that proposed accuracy comparison cannot attribute the behavior to contamination. Matching **all adaptive response distributions** extends the condition beyond TwinContrast’s summary statistic to every permitted black-box test.

If full adaptive behavioral equivalence truly holds, any benchmark–twin gap calculated from permitted responses also matches. Stating both makes the connection to the accuracy-gap question explicit; it should not be read as though gap matching alone establishes the broader impossibility.
So if the gaps match but the answers to individual questions differ, the claim about every black-box test does not follow?

Correct. A test allowed to examine individual answers might use a difference that the aggregate accuracy gap conceals. Equal gaps limit inference from the gap, not necessarily inference from every permitted response.

The hypothesis’s universal conclusion depends on the stronger premise: the clean alternative reproduces the contaminated alternative’s **entire distribution of observable adaptive interactions**. Without that premise, it would be too broad to say no black-box test can do better.
What does it mean to reproduce an adaptive response distribution? Is it enough to match the response to each question in isolation?

Not necessarily. An adaptive evaluator can choose its next query after observing an earlier answer. Matching each question’s answer distribution in isolation need not match the joint behavior that such an evaluator observes.

The required equivalence can be stated in terms of complete interaction transcripts: for every permitted adaptive querying policy, the contaminated and clean alternatives induce the same distribution over the queries chosen and responses received. Equivalently, a sufficiently strong conditional formulation requires matching the response distribution for every permitted next query after every permitted interaction history.
If the evaluator randomizes its choice of queries, does that leave room to distinguish the training histories?

Not under the stated premise. The evaluator can randomize and adapt, but it applies the same permitted policy regardless of which hidden training history is present. If that policy generates identically distributed observable transcripts under the clean and contaminated alternatives, its randomization cannot reveal which history occurred.

Randomization may matter when observable distributions differ. The hypothesis specifically concerns the case in which they match for **all** adaptive policies in scope.
Could a test choose to stop based on earlier responses and somehow beat the limit?

No, if the stopping decision uses only the permitted interaction and the complete transcript distributions match. Stopping early, continuing to query, or issuing a contamination flag are all decisions made from the evaluator’s observations and its own randomness. Identically distributed observations give the same probability of each such decision under the two alternatives.

That conclusion is conditional on full adaptive behavioral equivalence; it should not be inferred from equality on a fixed set of benchmark and twin items alone.
Can you make the power-versus-false-positive argument as short as possible?

Let the positive-flag event be whatever outcome a black-box test calls “contamination.” If the contaminated and clean alternatives yield the same distribution of all information available to that test, the event has the **same probability** under each alternative. The first probability is detection power; the second is the false-positive rate. Hence, for that pair of alternatives, **power equals FPR**, and in particular cannot exceed it.
The wording says “no black-box test exceeds its false-positive rate.” Does that mean no test can ever have power above 5%?

No. The statement applies **under the hypothesized equivalence** between a contaminated alternative and an admissible clean alternative. If a test is constrained to **5% FPR** for that clean alternative, it has at most **5% power against the equivalent contaminated alternative**. It says nothing comparable about contaminated models whose permitted behavior differs from every admitted clean alternative.

It also does not require fixing FPR at 5% to make the logical point. Whatever false-positive rate a given test has for the matching clean alternative is also its power for the behaviorally matching contaminated one.
If a test always calls a model contaminated, isn't its power greater than its false-positive rate?

No. Such a test would flag both alternatives every time: **100% power and 100% false positives** for the matched pair. It cannot obtain a detection advantage by issuing more flags. The impossibility concerns discrimination, not the bare ability to produce positive decisions.
Does the premise require knowing the actual training examples of either model?

No. It is framed in terms of two possible training histories and their observable consequences. The clean training is assumed to be admissible and to reproduce the relevant contaminated behavior; the black-box test itself need not know either history.

That is also why the statement should remain conditional. Unknown training distributions leave open possible alternatives, but their being unknown does not, by itself, establish that a behaviorally equivalent clean alternative exists in a particular case.
How does capability matching fit this hypothesis?

For the false-positive comparison to address contamination rather than broad differences in ability, the hypothesized clean alternative should be among the **uncontaminated, capability-matched models** the evaluation claims to distinguish from contaminated ones. If such an admitted clean model reproduces all permitted adaptive behavior of a contaminated model, no black-box rule can distinguish that pair while maintaining a lower positive-flag rate for the clean one.

The premise is about admissible alternatives. It should not be expanded to a clean comparator outside the intended class without saying why that comparator belongs in the claim’s scope.
What if the false-positive rate is specified only as an average across clean models?

Then the scope of the conclusion needs care. Behavioral equivalence guarantees that the power against a particular contaminated model equals the flagging probability for its matching **particular clean alternative**. An average FPR across a population of clean models does not necessarily bound that particular clean model’s flagging probability.

For an at-most-5% conclusion for the matched pair, the 5% false-positive constraint must apply to that clean comparator, or a suitable bound must otherwise cover it. The core hypothesis—no advantage over the comparator’s own false-positive rate—remains intact.
Could more benchmark/private-twin pairs separate the models if their present gaps match?

If only the present, finite-sample gaps match, more pairs could reveal a difference. That limited match is not the hypothesis’s full premise.

If clean training reproduces the contaminated alternative’s permitted adaptive response distributions, then querying additional permissible benchmark/private-twin pairs produces no identifying difference either. The evaluator may learn the shared behavior more precisely, but not which of the two training histories caused it.
What if the gaps differ a little but the complete adaptive behavior is otherwise described as identical?

If the accuracy gaps are calculated from permitted observations, differing gap distributions mean the complete permitted behavioral distributions are **not** identical. Both premises cannot hold in that sense. A small difference would move the question from exact equivalence to how much discrimination is possible given that difference.

The stated hypothesis addresses exact replication of the gaps and all adaptive response distributions. It does not assign a numerical detection bound to nearly equivalent alternatives.
Is the impossibility about TwinContrast specifically, or all black-box tests?

It has two scopes. Replicating the benchmark–twin accuracy-gap observations defeats identification from **TwinContrast’s gap-based comparison**. Replicating **all** permitted adaptive response distributions supports the stronger conclusion about **any black-box test restricted to those permitted interactions**.

The stronger premise matters because another test might look beyond aggregate accuracy. The hypothesis includes it so the conclusion is not confined to TwinContrast.
Could a black-box test infer contamination from the fact that the two models have different training histories, even if their behavior matches?

Not from black-box evidence alone. The difference in training histories defines which alternative is contaminated, but it is not an observation available to the test. If every permitted adaptive interaction has the same distribution under both histories, the evaluator cannot assign different positive-flag probabilities based on those interactions.

Information about training provenance from outside the permitted black-box setting would be a different kind of evidence, not an exception to this conditional black-box claim.
Does behavioral equivalence say the contaminated material had no causal effect on the contaminated model?

No. The hypothesis concerns what can be **observed and attributed**, not whether exposure had no causal effect. A contaminated model’s behavior could match a clean model’s behavior for different underlying reasons. Identical permitted observations do not reveal what the contaminated model would have done without exposure.

The conclusion is that the black-box test cannot distinguish the two specified histories, even if their causal histories differ.
Do we have to require the clean model to match a contaminated model on every conceivable language-model task?

The equivalence must cover **every query and adaptive interaction the claimed black-box test is permitted to use**. If the claim is about all black-box tests with unrestricted permissible queries, that is correspondingly broad. If the evaluation is restricted to particular observations, equivalence and the impossibility conclusion are limited to that observation scope.

It would be inaccurate to infer unrestricted behavioral identity merely from matching benchmark/private-twin accuracy gaps.
Is “no black-box test exceeds its false-positive rate” meant as a statistical tendency or an exact implication?

Under exact equality of the permitted adaptive observation distributions, it is an **exact conditional implication** for each test and matched clean–contaminated pair: the positive-flag probabilities are equal. The hypothesis is about whether the stated equivalence premise can hold for the alternatives being considered; it is not a report that any particular models have been shown to satisfy it.

Sampling uncertainty about observed accuracy gaps is a separate issue. Observing similar finite-sample gaps is not itself proof of the exact premise.
How does this answer the question about unknown training distributions and sample size?

It identifies the regime in which sample size cannot help: an **admissible clean training distribution** yields a capability-matched model whose benchmark–twin gap behavior and **all permitted adaptive response distributions** match those of the contaminated alternative. Any number of additional permitted observations still has the same distribution under both histories, so no black-box test gains detection power over its false-positive rate for that pair.

If unknown clean training distributions do *not* permit such a replica, or if more observations reveal a difference, the premise does not apply. The hypothesis marks an identifiability boundary rather than claiming that all contamination lies beyond it.
Can you state the hypothesis in one sentence without presenting clean replication as an established finding?

“**Hypothesis:** If an admissible clean training distribution reproduces a contaminated model’s benchmark–twin accuracy gaps and every permitted adaptive black-box response distribution, then no black-box test can attain detection power greater than its false-positive rate against that clean alternative.”

I want to contrast TwinContrast’s 74% power at 300 pairs with its 85% power at 500 pairs, then prove adaptive indistinguishability for response-equivalent clean and contaminated models. How do those parts of the plan fit together?

They address two different questions. The **74%-versus-85% comparison at 300 versus 500 pairs** concerns observed detection performance as the amount of paired evaluation material differs. The proposed proof concerns a boundary that more paired material cannot overcome: if an admissible clean model and a contaminated model are response-equivalent for every permitted adaptive black-box interaction, their training histories cannot be distinguished through those interactions.

The first part should describe what the two power figures show without attributing their difference solely to pair count. The second part should make precise what “response-equivalent” must cover and then establish the consequence for any adaptive detector. This is a plan for the comparison and proof, not a claim that the proof has been completed.
What is the numerical contrast between the two power figures?

The figure at **500 pairs is 11 percentage points higher** than the figure at **300 pairs**: 85% minus 74%. The paired-material counts differ by **200 pairs**. Those are arithmetic descriptions of the reported comparison, not an estimate that each additional pair contributed a fixed amount of power.
Should I present the increase as the effect of adding 200 pairs?

Not without an assumption that the two assessments are otherwise comparable in the ways relevant to power. The plan is to **contrast** 74% at 300 pairs with 85% at 500 pairs. That establishes which figure belongs to which count, but the two numbers alone do not isolate a causal effect of adding pairs.

A careful comparison can keep the relevant conditions attached to each estimate, including the TwinContrast accuracy-gap comparison and its clean-model calibration, without asserting an unreported mechanism for the difference.
Both figures concern the answer-only comparison we’ve been discussing. How much of that context needs to appear?

Enough to identify what is being compared: these are **TwinContrast detection-power figures** for the benchmark/private-twin accuracy comparison, rather than percentages of individual answers found. The stated assessments concern **30% answer-only contamination**, **one-point clean-model benchmark–twin gap drift**, and power at **5% FPR**. Keeping those conditions visible helps prevent a comparison of the figures from sounding like a claim about all contamination regimes.

The plan does not require reconstructing the underlying item responses or assigning a reason for the difference between the estimates.
Could the 74% and 85% instead mean that those fractions of the pairs revealed contamination?

No. They are **power figures**: rates at which TwinContrast flags the specified contaminated condition in the relevant assessments. The **300 and 500 pairs** are amounts of benchmark/private-twin evaluation material. The figures do not say how many individual pairs were diagnostic or how many contaminated answers were located.
Why put the power contrast before the impossibility proof?

It makes the distinction between **more information within an informative comparison** and **no identifying information under behavioral equivalence** especially clear. The two power figures show what is reported for two amounts of paired material. The proposed proof asks whether additional paired material—or adaptive querying—can ever help when clean and contaminated alternatives generate the same permitted response behavior.

That ordering is explanatory. It does not mean the empirical contrast establishes the proof’s premise, or that the proof explains the particular numerical difference between 74% and 85%.
What exactly needs to be equivalent for the proof? Is matching the benchmark–twin accuracy gap enough?

No. Matching the accuracy gap is enough to defeat identification **from that gap alone**, but another black-box test might use individual answers, response variability, or queries outside the paired material. For the planned claim about adaptive black-box tests, response equivalence must cover the **full distribution of permitted observations under every permitted adaptive querying policy**.

The proof should make that scope explicit. It must not infer an unrestricted impossibility merely from equal TwinContrast summary values.
