The impossibility applies at the observation scope actually covered by equivalence. To claim a limit for every permitted adaptive test, the equality must extend to the distributions of complete permitted adaptive transcripts.
If two models match on both named probes, is that enough?

It would limit inference from those probes if their **complete joint observation distributions** match. It would not, merely by matching their reported summaries, rule out a difference accessible through other permitted black-box queries.

The report should distinguish an audit-specific inability to separate histories from the stronger impossibility for all permitted adaptive interactions. The artifact description names the response-equivalence impossibility but does not identify a particular pair of models as satisfying its premise.
Can an adaptive evaluator evade the impossibility by choosing a follow-up question?

Not if response equivalence covers the **complete distribution of permitted adaptive interactions**, including follow-up queries chosen from earlier answers. In that case every decision derived from the transcript occurs with the same probability under the two histories.

If equivalence has been shown only for a fixed collection of questions, the broader adaptive conclusion does not follow. The observation scope is part of the condition, not a detail to omit.
Does response equivalence imply that contamination had no effect on training?

No. It says that the permitted black-box observations cannot tell the contaminated history from an admissible clean alternative. It does not reveal the contaminated model’s behavior in a counterfactual world without exposure, or establish that the two models have the same internal processes.

The impossibility is about identifying provenance from behavior, not about ruling out a causal role for training material.
Does the report’s impossibility result negate whatever power it documents?

No. It applies when its **response-equivalence premise** holds. Detection power may be documented for assessed conditions that do produce an observable distinction from the relevant clean comparison. The report description provides no numerical power values and does not say that those assessed conditions are response-equivalent.

The careful reading keeps a conditional limit separate from performance measurements made under specified assumptions.
Can 500 pairs or 800 items overcome the equivalence limit?

Not if additional permitted observations from those pairs or items remain identically distributed for the clean and contaminated alternatives. More material can improve discrimination when there is a real behavioral difference to observe; it cannot reveal different training histories from observations whose complete distributions match.

The counts specify the material covered by the report, not exceptions to the response-equivalence argument.
Does the report determine whether every unknown training distribution is covered by the transport assumptions?

The description does not say that. It tells us the assumptions are documented, not that they have been established for every possible clean training distribution. A conditional conclusion must identify the clean targets and controls for which transport is justified.

Unknown distributions are precisely why the coverage of those assumptions matters: a clean model outside the covered class might reproduce a purported contamination signal or have a different false-positive probability.
How would a reader avoid mistaking the report for an unconditional certification?

Keep each kind of statement attached to its conditions. The **500-pair and 800-item** performance documentation needs the relevant contaminated and clean comparisons; any FPR transfer needs the stated transport assumptions and clean distractor-exposure limits; the impossibility needs a response-equivalent clean–contaminated pair and a specified observation scope.

The report’s existence is not itself proof that a particular performance threshold was met or that all those assumptions hold universally.
Could it report a satisfactory FPR while leaving power unresolved?

Conceptually, yes: control of false flags and detection of contamination are distinct questions. But the artifact description does not tell us whether either quantity is satisfactory or unresolved; it says the report **documents both power and FPR**. Without its values and conditions, we should not assign it a performance judgment.
Likewise, could good power coexist with an inadequate transport assumption?

Yes, in principle. A detector could flag contaminated models frequently in an assessed comparison while lacking a justified FPR guarantee for a broader set of clean targets. Power does not prove that negative controls bound clean target–control mismatch.

That conceptual distinction explains why the report documents both performance and transport assumptions. It is not a claim that the report found either problem.
Does documenting distractor-exposure limits tell us the first exposure level at which calibration fails?

No such threshold is specified in this artifact description. A limit on the scope of a conditional inference is not automatically the exact point where a detector’s actual false-positive rate first exceeds a target. The report’s documented limits should not be expanded into a performance curve or a sharp failure boundary without the corresponding data.
What should I say if someone asks for the report’s exact power and FPR percentages?

Say that the description identifies **power and FPR as documented contents** for the **500-pair/800-item audit**, but it does **not supply their numerical values**. Providing particular percentages from the description would invent a result. The same restraint applies to the outcomes of any transport checks not stated here.
What is the shortest faithful description of the artifact?

The **conditional audit report** documents **power and FPR using 500 TwinContrast pairs and 800 DistractorRecall items**, its **transport assumptions** and **independent distractor-exposure limits**, and the **impossibility of distinguishing response-equivalent clean and contaminated models from the permitted black-box behavior**.
